Very compressed for its length. 'In a long south-westerly' expects the reader to supply the elided noun (gale/blow), and 'A head that gives back nothing' reuses 'head' from the first sentence's 'window head' several lines later.

The sentence 'The water ... runs down into the cavity, onto a tray ... which discharges it through the open joints' states the general case before the very next sentence qualifies it for windy conditions; a fast reader could carry the wrong tense of the claim into the question. The stem's 'before the wind drops' is what disambiguates it.

The arithmetic reconciles exactly, which is what makes the item fair: a beast taken up on Monday waits six nights for the Sunday crying (6 x 6d = 3s, plus the 1s taking-up fee = 4s), one taken up on Saturday waits one night (6d + 1s = 1s 6d). Same counting convention both times, so there is no ambiguity to argue about.

The inference the item wants - the bill is set by the notice schedule rather than by the owner - is genuinely earned, and 'neither owner disputed the reckoning' closes off the escape route that one of the figures was simply an error.

'Pinder' is never glossed and is not recoverable from a modern reader's vocabulary, though 'The pinder's office carried no wage: Jabez Skellorne had the fees instead' makes the role clear enough from context.

Option C is the strongest foil - it offers a tidy causal story (heavy bill = careless owner) that the passage specifically refutes, since both owners came the day they were cried. Option D is defeated only by the word 'decided', since the vestry, not Skellorne, fixed when notice was given.
Period register (vestry, common, taken up, cried at the church door) is consistent and unforced.
